paragraphs.text: Good afternoon, sisters and elders. I'm excited to begin district interviews tomorrow. I look very much forward to speaking with each of you personally over the next few days. I don't have any specific assignments for you, but I may surprise you with a request or two in the course of our visit, so be prepared as much as you can be. I love having these interviews and I know you're going to enjoy this as well. So don't fear. Don't worry. Enjoy this talk together.

I'm really grateful for the technology that we've been blessed with that allows for our effective communication even with this lockdown. I'm so very grateful that you are using your energy so well and putting it into the work—everything that you can to keep building the kingdom. We had 13 baptisms last weekend. We're projecting another 12 or 13 or 14 next weekend. I'm stunned by that. I'm just so excited, so proud of you. So very grateful for your innovative, intelligent, diligent, faithful service.

So I know that you really weren't planning on this kind of a mission when you filled out your papers. And that's all the more impressive to me that you have embraced what's happened without becoming chronic complainers and whiners. I know some of you have told me that you complained too much and that's one of your goals to stop doing some complaining, and that's a worthy goal for sure. But you're doing well.

I do have a concern. There's been some things that have started to come up lately. I'm hearing and reading in your letters really more of a judging spirit than we used to have on our mission. Now I can understand the temptation to engage in the judger mindset since you have been together for so very long and you're together all day long. You don't have an opportunity to interact with others very often and that can create the opportunity to kind of get into that wrong mindset.

However, elders and sisters, it is a very unhealthy mindset. It just won't do you any good. Judges never really feel very good about themselves. Even when their judgment's accurate—I mean, you can be judging somebody to doing something wrong and you can be right about your judgment—it won't make you feel good. And here's something else: it won't make the wrong thing right, and it won't make the person who's doing the wrong thing want to do right. Judging just doesn't work for you and me, which is probably why the Lord says judgment is left up to the Lord, because he has the ability to judge perfectly and we simply do not.

And I found in my own life that while I have to make judgment calls at my calling or in my business, when it comes to judging people, it's just better not done. It's better to explain, understand, listen. Certainly decisions have to be made, but the judging part needs to go away because it's not helpful—not helpful to you, not helpful to the other person.
Here's a couple of common examples of how judging and fault finding can easily begin with even really good missionaries.

Example one: Elder A was transferred to his new companion, Elder B, just last transfer. They've been together about seven weeks. Over the first few weeks, Elder A and Elder B got along really well together. They discovered they had some common interests and shared some high goals and really enjoyed those first few weeks. But as the weeks went by, Elder A started seeing some of Elder B's weaknesses. He noticed that Elder B didn't wash the dishes the way he thought they should be washed. He also noticed that Elder B took a long time in the shower. Elder A started to spend more and more time thinking about Elder B's faults and those faults seemed to grow in importance to Elder A. He became more irritable and short-tempered with Elder B. Pretty soon Elder A even started talking to his kababayans about Elder B in a not very kind way. The strange thing is that each week that went past, Elder B seemed to do more of the very things that irritated Elder A. And eventually they had to have an emergency transfer with both elders not understanding what went wrong. You can think about that example. You can think about what might have been a solution to that problem that ended up being a problem where those two missionaries probably never ever saw themselves as friends in the mission field or even after the mission field. Very sad.

Example two: Two sisters were companions and they were having great success. The reason was because they were so dedicated and diligent. They really loved serving together and they were the best of friends and they were good at missionary work. Then one day one of the sisters said something to a member about her companion. It wasn't a bad thing, but it was misunderstood by the member who then told it to others. It got back to the companion. She was very hurt and offended about what she thought her companion had said about her to the member. She stopped talking with her companion, even said some unkind things to other members about her companion. Of course, these comments found their way back to the first missionary and soon there was no love left in the companionship. The success they had been having dried up and went away. And when a transfer came, they were both so happy to no longer be together. Again, what a tragedy. How sad that it could be so great and end so bad because... well, you figure out why the because.

Modern prophets and scriptures warn us that finding fault, pointing fingers, judging others can be spiritually hazardous. There are many scriptural warnings about fault finding and judging. Two of the most pointed are from the Savior Himself. In Matthew chapter 7 verses 1 through 5 we read: "Judge not, that ye be not judged. For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again. And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye? Or how wilt thou say to thy brother, Let me pull out the mote out of thine eye; and, behold, a beam is in thine own eye? Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye."

Without realizing it, we might find ourselves being like the Pharisees who brought the woman caught in adultery to Jesus. We compare ourselves favorably to the people who were caught doing something wrong because we think our sins and mistakes are private and nobody knows about them. We must always remember that God knows our secrets and He knows our sins. And when we condemn or find fault with others, He is always watching and observing us. Perhaps this is why when Jesus said to the Pharisees, "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone at her," all those accusers silently left because they were indicted in their own hearts by the Spirit of God. They saw clearly their own sins.

If we ridicule others believing that our sins are hidden from them, we become hypocrites like the scribes and the Pharisees, whom Jesus likened to, quote, "whited sepulchres, which indeed appear beautiful outward, but are within full of dead men's bones, and of all uncleanness," close quote. Finally, when we criticize and find fault with others, our view can be distorted because we often see our own weaknesses in others. The Apostle Paul warned of this tendency, quote, "Therefore thou art inexcusable, O man, whosoever thou art that judgest: for wherein thou judgest another, thou condemnest thyself; for thou that judgest doest the same things," close quote. If we project our flaws onto others, perhaps our attitude toward them is a measurement of our own poor performance.
I've often found wise instruction in our hymns. Perhaps the next time you feel inclined to judge or find fault, you should turn in the hymnbook to hymn 235. It goes like this:

Should you feel inclined to censure
Faults you may in others view,
Ask your own heart, ere you venture,
If you have not failings too.
Let not friendly vows be broken;
Rather strive a friend to gain;
Many a word in anger spoken
Finds its passage home again.

Elders and sisters, we should all of us in the Quezon City North Mission be the best of friends. We should all see the best in each other. If we see something that's not really up to missionary standards, our first thing should be in a loving way to go to our brother or sister and say, "I noticed this. Was I wrong in what I thought I saw? Or is there any way that I can help out?" Our first intention should be to help our fellow missionaries in this mission to rise above their weaknesses, not to pin them down with their weaknesses. We want to be able to have reunions in the years to come where each and every one of you are overjoyed to see all the other missionaries because you have become the warmest friends.

So do unto others, dear sisters and elders, as you would have others do to you. As you follow that simple rule, you will have peace in your heart and hope in your future and no regrets in your past. Good night. I love you.
